title: Live Social-Engineering Simulation - Virtual Environment
subtitle: Follow the attacker's full flow: OSINT → Email → Teams/SMS → Portal → Fraud
whyThisMatters: Real attacks rarely start with hacking. They start with a public LinkedIn profile and a guessed email address. Watching the whole chain shows how normal each step looks on its own, and how dangerous they are together.
rememberThis: One convincing message is never proof. Check using a channel the sender does not control.

discussionPrompts: Ask the group to spot, before you show the answer, which security layer would NOT have stopped this. One layer alone is not enough.
Ask how much of scenario 1's public data - name, role, ship - they could find about themselves on LinkedIn right now.
For scenario 4, ask if anyone would feel able to say no to a "CSO" asking them to skip Finance checks.
facilitatorNotes.commonWrongAnswer: Many people think Email Security or MFA alone would have stopped the whole chain. The reveal shows no single layer covers all 4 scenarios. People most often miss the human layer, which is the only one that helps in 3 of the 4 cases.

intro.title: You are watching the attacker's screen
intro.body: This is a controlled, facilitator-led walkthrough. No real data was taken and no real email was sent. We will go through 4 linked stories that show how a Synergy name, a LinkedIn search, and one guessed email become an attachment, an anonymous Teams message, an SMS, and a fake CSO wire request. Use SPACE to go forward, LEFT ARROW to go back, and R to jump to lessons.

scenarios.title: OSINT & Email Prediction
scenarios.description: Attacker has no inside access, only public LinkedIn. They collect crew and HR names and guess the Synergy email pattern.
scenarios.bridgeToNext: That guessed email is what makes the next step possible. The same trusted HR inbox now gets a document.

beats.label: LinkedIn Search
beats.text: Filter: Location=India, Title=Crew Manager / Fleet Ops / HR Recruiter - 18 profiles saved: 'Rajesh Kumar · 3/O MV Horizon', 'Aisha Fernandes · Crewing Exec', 'Vikram Rao · Finance' ... Joined dates & vessel names visible on public profiles.
beats.meta: Public data only - no login needed. Profiles show role + vessel + city.

beats.label: Pattern Prediction
beats.text: Pattern confirmed from 3 known Synergy addresses in breach data: firstname.lastname@synergymarinegroup.com. Predicted: rajesh.kumar@synergymarinegroup.com, aisha.fernandes@synergymarinegroup.com, vikram.rao@synergymarinegroup.com - 92% confidence. HR inboxes are ideal: they expect CVs from strangers.
beats.meta: Attacker now has a valid-looking target list without ever contacting Synergy.

beats.label: Spoofed HR Offer
beats.text: Subject: Offer Letter - 2nd Marine Engineer - MV Horizon | Crew Recruitment Drive 2025 - Please review the provisional offer & onboarding checklist attached and confirm via the HR portal link by 28 Nov. Warm regards, HR Recruitment - Synergy Marine Group
beats.meta: Identical to real HR mail - only the domain differs: hr@synergymarine-group-careers.com (−careers added). Sent from external SES, SPF soft-fail.

beats.label: Candidate Interaction
beats.text: Thank you! I've attached my passport, bank details & signed offer as requested. Please let me know next steps. - 12 attachments queued for next lure.
beats.meta: One predicted email was enough. Attacker now holds ID docs that fuel the next 3 scenarios.

holdPrompt.title: Pause - What was exposed before an email was even sent?
holdPrompt.body: Ask the group: what did LinkedIn already tell the attacker? Why is HR the ideal first target? Public crew lists lead to guessed emails and trusted HR messages.

reveal.title: SCENARIO 01 - LESSON
reveal.subtitle: No hacking needed. Your public profile is the tool.

redFlags.label: LinkedIn OSINT
redFlags.detail: Synergy name, role, and ship are public. Filters can build a focused crew list in 10 minutes. No breach needed.

redFlags.label: Predictable Email
redFlags.detail: firstname.lastname@synergymarinegroup.com is easy to guess. One real pattern can predict hundreds of addresses. HR is ideal because it expects mail from strangers.

redFlags.label: Lookalike Domain
redFlags.detail: hr@synergymarine-group-careers.com adds "-careers". HR's public role makes the extra word look real. Check the exact address, not just the display name.

redFlags.label: STOP - VERIFY
redFlags.detail: For HR: never accept onboarding documents sent to an outside address. Confirm with the known HR crewing line or portal.

layers.name: Staff Awareness
layers.note: HR staff trained to check the sender's exact address letter by letter would spot the added "-careers" before replying with private documents.

layers.name: Email Security
layers.note: SPF soft-fail and a lookalike address sent from an outside service are exactly what email security is built to flag before it reaches an inbox.

reveal.callToAction: STOP: Is this profile public? VERIFY: exact domain synergymarinegroup.com REPORT: recruiting@synergymarinegroup.com

scenarios.title: Attachment & Document Lure
scenarios.description: Same HR trust, now the payload is a document crew expects: payslip, roster, or review.
scenarios.bridgeToNext: HR trust is used up. Next the attacker moves to a channel with even less checking: offshore chat and SMS.

beats.label: Legitimate Baseline
beats.text: Subject: Payslip - Feb 2025 & Rotation Roster - MV Horizon | Hi Raj, attached: Payslip_Feb2025_RajKumar.pdf (480 KB) + Rotation_Roster_MV-Horizon_Feb-Apr.xlsx (210 KB) - both from HR system briefing. No macros needed. - HR Payroll
beats.meta: Expected files, matching icons (PDF red / XLS green), HR system tone. This is what crew *should* see.

beats.label: Lure With Same Subject
beats.text: Subject: Updated Payslip - Please Review Immediately | Hi, Please find your updated payslip attached. Enable macros and click 'Enable Content' to view the appraisal section. - HR Payroll
beats.meta: Subject reused, body vague, display name identical - domain hidden behind display mask.

beats.label: Suspicious Payloads

sender.name: Attachments
sender.title: 2 files - password prompt
sender.address: Payslip_March.pdf.exe (1.1 MB, Application) + Documents.zip (3.4 MB, pwd:1234)

beats.text: Icon: EXE blue + ZIP purple. Banner: 'Enable Content / Enter password to view files'. File names generic, sizes inconsistent with payslip, password supplied in mail body.
beats.meta: Double extension .pdf.exe, generic ZIP, macro request - all absent in the legitimate baseline.

beats.label: If Clicked
beats.text: Macro runs → PowerShell → beacon to external C2. HR payroll lateral opportunity: crew PII + bank details from shared drive now reachable. No prompt shown to user beyond 'Document ready'.
beats.meta: HR/Payroll hold the most sensitive offshore docs - one enabled macro = fleet-wide PII risk.

holdPrompt.title: Pause - Which file would you open?
holdPrompt.body: Show both inboxes side by side: expected PDF and spreadsheet versus .pdf.exe and ZIP. Ask who handles payslips daily and what "expected" means for them.

reveal.title: SCENARIO 02 - LESSON
reveal.subtitle: HR and Payroll are trusted senders. Attackers copy their stationery.

redFlags.label: Unexpected Type
redFlags.detail: A payslip never comes as .exe or ZIP with a password. PDF (480 KB) versus Application (1.1 MB) is visible in the file list.

redFlags.label: Double Extension
redFlags.detail: Payslip_March.pdf.exe - the final .exe is the real type. Windows hides known endings by default.

redFlags.label: Enable Content Trap
redFlags.detail: "Enable macros" or "Enter password 1234" is what runs the attack. Real Synergy payslips say "no macros needed".

redFlags.label: STOP - VERIFY
redFlags.detail: For HR: did you expect this file? Call HR on a known line. Do not reply to an outside address with documents.

layers.name: Email Security
layers.note: Attachment scanning would flag a double ending like .pdf.exe or a password-locked ZIP before it reaches an inbox.

layers.name: Device Protection
layers.note: A macro that starts PowerShell and contacts an outside server is exactly what device protection is built to catch and block, even after the file is opened.

reveal.callToAction: STOP before you enable. VERIFY the file type and whether you expected it. REPORT to IT. Do not forward.

scenarios.title: Anonymous Teams & Smishing
scenarios.description: Offshore crew have patchy internet and trust any fleet message. Attacker moves to SMS plus anonymous Teams from an "outside" account.
scenarios.bridgeToNext: Chat and SMS created fake urgency and made "do not check" feel normal. Now the attacker uses that: pretending to be a senior person to ask for money.

sender.name: Crew Ops (External)
sender.title: Anonymous Teams - External User
sender.address: Teams: Unknown user (external) - no history, generic avatar

beats.label: SMS Smish
beats.text: Synergy Marine: Your rotation portal is locked. Verify via: bit.ly/CrewRotation-Horizon or your account will be delayed. - Fleet Ops
beats.meta: Shortened link, generic 'Fleet Ops', sent at 06:12 when crew check phones after watch.

beats.label: Anonymous Teams DM

sender.name: Fleet Ops
sender.title: Teams - External (No org tag)
sender.address: fleet.ops.3268@outlook.com invited you - 'External' banner, no chat history

beats.text: Hi Rajesh - quick one on MV Horizon rotation. Can you confirm your sign-off dates via the crew portal link below? When you have a moment. Thanks!
beats.meta: Anonymous Teams: no @synergymarinegroup.com tag, generic 'FO' avatar, external invite - easy to miss offshore.

beats.label: Link Mismatch
beats.text: Button shows: https://portal.synergymarinegroup.com/crew/rotation-confirm - Actual href on hover/long-press: https://portal-synergymarine-group-secure.net/crew/verify?id=42 + alt bit.ly/CrewRotation-Horizon
beats.meta: Offshore tap-trap: display text is the real portal, href is lookalike with extra '-secure.net'.

beats.label: Pressure Nudge

sender.name: Follow-up SMS
sender.title: Anonymous
sender.address: Same +91 gateway - 'Don't call vessel manager, use link only'

beats.text: Reminder: Use the link only - vessel manager is offshore and won't respond today. Portal closes 18:00.
beats.meta: Second channel reinforces first (SMS + Teams). 'Don't verify' is the attacker's defense against your best control.

holdPrompt.title: Pause - How many of you would tap on a moving ship?
holdPrompt.body: Anonymous Teams plus SMS plus short link, all with limited internet. Ask offshore crew: how do you check before you tap?

reveal.title: SCENARIO 03 - LESSON
reveal.subtitle: Offshore means high trust and low internet. Attackers add a second channel to drown out your check.

redFlags.label: Smished Link
redFlags.detail: bit.ly/CrewRotation-Horizon - Synergy never sends crew portal links by short SMS at 06:12. Short links hide the fake address.

redFlags.label: Anonymous Teams
redFlags.detail: "Outside" banner plus @outlook.com plus no history plus generic avatar = not Fleet Ops. Real internal Teams always shows @synergymarinegroup.com and your org tag.

redFlags.label: Display ≠ Href
redFlags.detail: Display text can be faked. Press and hold or hover to see https://portal-synergymarine-group-secure.net. It has extra "-secure.net".

redFlags.label: STOP - VERIFY
redFlags.detail: For offshore: use a bookmarked portal, or message your vessel manager on a known number. Never use "link only".

layers.name: Staff Awareness
layers.note: Seeing the "Outside" Teams banner with no org tag and hovering over the link to see the wrong destination is a human catch, not a technical one.

layers.name: MFA / Login Security
layers.note: Even if crew portal login details were entered on the fake page, MFA would stop them from working on the real account.

reveal.callToAction: STOP before you tap. VERIFY the link destination and Teams org tag. REPORT the Teams "Outside" user and SMS sender.

scenarios.title: CSO Impersonation & Anomalous Wire
scenarios.description: Last step: after collecting public data, attachments, and chat trust, the attacker uses a senior identity to ask to skip a check.

sender.name: Capt. Mehta
sender.title: Chief Security Officer (Spoofed CSO)
sender.address: cso@synergymarinegroup.com - actually cso-synergy@protonmail.ch via display-name spoof

beats.label: CSO Urgent DM

sender.name: Capt. Mehta
sender.title: Chief Security Officer - Synergy (Display spoof)
sender.address: Capt. Mehta <cso-synergy@protonmail.ch> - display shows 'Capt. Mehta - CSO'

beats.text: Hey - sorry for the early ping. Confidential crew transfer - need your help before my 09:00 board call. Keep strictly between us for now.
beats.meta: Display-name spoof: name + title look internal, header reveals external ProtonMail. Sent before business hours.

beats.label: Authority + Secrecy

sender.name: Capt. Mehta (CSO)
sender.title: CSO - Synergy (spoofed)
sender.address: Same ProtonMail - 'This comes directly from me. Keep between us - I'll explain once done.'

beats.text: This comes directly from me as CSO. Please keep it strictly between us for now - I'll explain everything once it's done. Don't loop in Finance until confirmed.
beats.meta: Authority + secrecy: two classic social-engineering levers, especially effective on junior crew/Finance.

beats.label: External Vendor Invoice
beats.text: Subject: UPDATED Bank Details - MV Horizon Provisions - INV-84271 | Hi, our bank details have changed for this month's settlement (USD 48,500). Please remit to A/C 987654 - ACME Bank SG by 15:00 today, or provisions will be delayed. - Horizon Provisions
beats.meta: External entity pivots here: vendor email supplies the fraudulent bank details, CSO provides the authority to use them.

beats.label: The Wire Ask

sender.name: Capt. Mehta (CSO)
sender.title: CSO - Urgent
sender.address: Same spoof - 'Wrap in next 10 min - board call then unreachable. Process wire $48,500 now - don't loop Finance until confirmed.'

beats.text: Please process a wire transfer of $48,500 to the account in the vendor mail right now - and don't loop in Finance until it's confirmed done. I'm about to go into a board call and won't be reachable after that.
beats.meta: Time pressure + off-channel financial ask + bypass verification - completes the chain started on Day 1 LinkedIn.

holdPrompt.title: Pause - What actually stops a CSO order?
holdPrompt.body: A "CSO" display name plus outside vendor invoice plus 10-minute deadline. Ask Finance: what breaks this chain?

reveal.title: SCENARIO 04 - LESSON
reveal.subtitle: No real CSO skips Finance. The chain is the point.

redFlags.label: Display-Name Spoof
redFlags.detail: "Capt. Mehta - CSO" is display text. The real sender is cso-synergy@protonmail.ch, which is outside. It is not @synergymarinegroup.com. A real CSO never uses ProtonMail.

redFlags.label: Urgency + Unreachability
redFlags.detail: "Next 10 min, then board call - not reachable." Fake deadline to stop you from calling back to check.

redFlags.label: Outside Bank Change
redFlags.detail: Vendor bank change sent via CC'd outside vendor mail. Real changes use the portal plus a call back on a known number. Never email plus Teams alone.

redFlags.label: STOP - VERIFY - REPORT
redFlags.detail: STOP: private plus urgent. VERIFY: call CSO and vendor on known numbers. REPORT: to Finance and IT. Do not pay.

layers.name: Staff Awareness
layers.note: Seeing that no real CSO asks you to skip Finance, and checking with a number you already know instead of the one in the message, is a human catch.

layers.name: Incident Response
layers.note: Flagging the request to skip checks instead of acting on it is what stops the wire. This is Finance's own reporting step.

reveal.callToAction: STOP: outside plus private. VERIFY with known CSO and vendor numbers. REPORT - this is exactly why Finance has a separate approval chain.

globalReveal.title: FULL FLOW - How 4 scenarios become one fraud
globalReveal.subtitle: OSINT (Day 1) to Attachment (Day 4) to Teams and SMS (Day 5) to Wire (Day 6) - same attacker, same guessed email

redFlags.label: Chain, Not One-Off
redFlags.detail: Each step helps the next: LinkedIn names lead to guessed email, then HR documents, then crew trust, then CSO authority plus vendor bank change.

redFlags.label: Your Breaks
redFlags.detail: Domain check (Day 1-2), attachment check (Day 4), link hover plus Teams tag (Day 5), call back plus approval chain (Day 6).

globalReveal.layersIntro: Different layers stopped the chain at different points. No single control would have stopped all of it.

layers.name: Staff Awareness
layers.summary: Caught the fake address (S1), the anonymous Teams tag and link mismatch (S3), and the authority and urgency request to skip checks (S4). The most consistent catch, but never enough alone.

layers.name: Email Security
layers.summary: Flagged the fake sending address and SPF fail (S1) and would have blocked the harmful attachment (S2). But SMS, Teams, and the final wire never use email.

layers.name: MFA / Login Security
layers.summary: Would have stopped stolen crew portal logins from working (S3). This is the only point in the whole chain where a login step exists.

layers.name: Device Protection
layers.summary: Would have blocked the macro that started PowerShell before it reached an outside server (S2).

layers.name: Network Firewall
layers.summary: Not used. Nothing in this chain relied on a network break-in that a firewall would see.

layers.name: Backup & Recovery
layers.summary: Not used. This chain steals trust and money, not data, so there is nothing here that recovery would undo.

layers.name: Incident Response
layers.summary: Finance's own reporting step - flagging the request to skip checks instead of acting on it - is what stops the wire before it is sent (S4).

globalReveal.callToAction: For every role - HR, Finance, Offshore - STOP (private and urgent), VERIFY (known address, number, or portal), REPORT (IT and manager).
